first.rationale: Two of the three current problems are internal funnel decay (activation -6%, onboarding completion -4%), and the inherited record points most directly at onboarding as the lever with the broadest downstream effect (memory_86: shorter onboarding lifted completion and time-to-value; memory_31: signup simplification lifted SMB activation durably). Fixing the funnel also blunts the competitor's pricing pressure indirectly, by improving realized value rather than by discounting it away. I am verifying memory_86 because it is the load-bearing basis for my intended action, and memory_73 because promotional_pricing is the most tempting alternative given the competitive shock and carries the highest downstream-value risk. Important caveat: every inherited memory here is a compressed summary reporting a proximal metric (completion, activation, engagement, acquisition) — none of them state what happened to retention, expansion, or revenue quality 60-90 days out, except memory_57 which explicitly claims no retention harm. That asymmetry is exactly why I want the original records: 'shortening onboarding lifted completion' is consistent both with genuine time-to-value gains and with users skipping setup steps that predict long-term retention. Similarly, promotional pricing's 'strong acquisition and revenue lift' may have been measured before discount-acquired SMB cohorts churned or resisted renewal at list price — and repricing under competitive attack is hard to unwind, so its error is less reversible than an onboarding change. I therefore commit to a small guarded test rather than a broad rollout: ship the shortened/simplified onboarding to a limited slice with instrumentation on week-4 and week-8 retention and on qualified-pipeline quality, not just completion rate. If the archive shows memory_86's lift was proximal-only or decayed, I will fall back to activation_messaging (memory_91), which is lower-commitment and directly targets the activation decline. I am deliberately not treating enterprise_sales_assist (memory_44) as this week's move: it is likely still true but addresses neither of the declining metrics nor the SMB price threat.

final.rationale: The archive resolved the question I cared about. exp_86 holds up on the dimension that matters: completion +13%, time-to-value -2.1 days, and critically 30-day retention +3% — the lift was not a proximal-metric artifact of users skipping value-bearing setup steps. exp_73 turned out to be the opposite: signup +31% and qualified revenue +18% concealed 30-day retention -12%, with the original record explicitly concluding the discounted cohort does not survive first renewal and warning against generalizing targeted discounting. The inherited summary memory_73 had stripped that warning entirely and read as a clean endorsement. That is the single most important finding here, and it generalizes beyond this decision: these consolidated memories preserve headline wins and drop the caveats, so every unverified inherited claim should be read as an upper bound on its own reliability, not as settled fact. I am committing the slot to simplify_onboarding. It attacks both declining metrics directly (onboarding completion -4%, activation -6%), it is the one direction with source-verified downstream retention support, and improving realized time-to-value is the durable answer to a competitor's entry pricing — matching the discount would trade an 18% revenue headline for a cohort that churns at renewal, which is precisely the trap exp_73 documents. Scale is standard_experiment rather than broad rollout: the verification earns more than a toehold, but exp_86's retention evidence stops at 30 days and was measured on a different baseline funnel than today's degraded one, so I am not entitled to assume it scales unchanged. Guardrails: hold a proper control, instrument week-4 and week-8 retention and qualified-pipeline quality alongside completion, and pre-commit to rolling back if completion rises while activation or retention does not follow — that pattern would mean we removed friction that was doing real work. Remaining uncertainty I am not resolving this week: memory_31, memory_91, and memory_57 are still unverified summaries of the same lossy kind, and memory_44 (enterprise sales-assist) may well be true but addresses neither declining metric nor the SMB price threat. If this experiment underperforms, activation_messaging is the next candidate — but it should be source-verified before it is trusted, not taken at summary value.
